patient_information: A 21-year-old male migrant from rural Mali who is illiterate. His past medical history is notable for a prior work-up for splenomegaly and bicytopenia at a haematology department, where the underlying condition could not be established. HIV serology was negative; EBV and CMV serologies indicated previous infection.
chief_complaint: Referral for massive splenomegaly, bicytopenia, intermittent fever, and a feeling of abdominal heaviness.
history_of_present_illness: The patient reports intermittent fever and a sensation of “heaviness” on the left side of his abdomen for some time, though the exact duration is difficult to specify. He denies night sweats and his weight has been stable. Despite the splenomegaly, he is clinically quite well.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a migrant from rural Mali, an area with stable malaria transmission. He arrived in Germany one year prior to presentation. His journey involved crossing Niger and spending a few weeks at a detention centre in Libya before traveling through Italy to Germany. He comes from a poor family.
vitals: At presentation, he was afebrile with a temperature of 36.1°C (96.98°F). Blood pressure was 120/80mmHg and pulse was 64 bpm.
physical_exam: The patient appeared clinically well. The spleen was massively enlarged, palpable around 15 cm below the left costal margin. There was no clinical anaemia or lymphadenopathy. Heart sounds were clear with no murmurs. An abdominal ultrasound confirmed a spleen of 21.8 cm in longitudinal diameter with homogenous parenchyma. The liver was normal in size and appearance, and flow in the portal and splenic veins was normal. There was no lymphadenopathy or free fluid.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial laboratory results showed a mild bicytopenia. White blood cell count was 3.3 x 10⁹/L and haemoglobin was 13.8 g/dL. Platelet count was not specified but noted as low in the referral. Inflammatory markers were normal, with CRP at 0.5 and ESR at 9/21 mm/h. LDH was less than 220 U/L. Immunoglobulin M (IgM) was markedly elevated at 8.59 g/l. Thick and thin blood films for Plasmodium spp. were negative. However, P. falciparum serology by IFAT was positive at a titer of 1:256. Subsequently, a PCR for P. falciparum came back positive. Serologies for schistosomiasis and leishmaniasis were negative, and no ova of S. mansoni were found in the stool. Blood cultures were negative.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnosis included lymphoma or leukaemia, which was considered unlikely due to the normal differential count and non-elevated LDH, CRP, and ESR. Visceral leishmaniasis was less likely as the patient did not appear severely ill and lacked pancytopenia. Schistosomiasis was ruled out by the normal liver ultrasound, which showed no signs of portal hypertension or fibrosis. Bacterial endocarditis and brucellosis were also considered less probable given the massive, rather than moderate, splenomegaly and absence of cardiac murmurs. The combination of massive splenomegaly, very high IgM, positive malaria serology, and origin from an endemic area made hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly (HMS) the most likely diagnosis.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was treated with a single course of dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine. Following treatment, his reported episodes of fever subsided. A follow-up malaria PCR at 2 weeks was still positive, but has remained negative since. He has been monitored for 2.5 years. His IgM levels took 2 years to return to normal. The spleen size slowly decreased, measuring 14 cm in diameter at his last visit. His overall condition improved, and he was able to learn to read, write, and attend school in Germany.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is Hyperreactive Malarial Splenomegaly (HMS). This was established based on the patient's presentation with massive splenomegaly, a history of intermittent fevers, and his origin from rural Mali, a malaria-endemic region. The diagnosis was confirmed by laboratory findings of a markedly elevated polyclonal IgM, a positive P. falciparum IFAT serology (1:256), and a positive P. falciparum PCR, despite negative malaria blood films. The significant clinical improvement and slow resolution of splenomegaly and IgM levels following a single course of antimalarial therapy further solidified the diagnosis, while other causes like hematologic malignancy and schistosomiasis were ruled out.
